# Neural Networks {#sec-Neural_Networks}
Neural networks are computational models inspired by the human brain's network of neurons. They consist of interconnected layers of artificial neurons that process information through weighted connections, learning to recognize complex patterns through training on data. While conceptually related to traditional statistical models, neural networks can capture highly non-linear relationships and interactions that would be difficult or impossible to specify manually. Neural networks are therefore a powerful tool for a wide range of applications, including image recognition, natural language processing, and time series forecasting. 

{{< include /Figures/Computational_Statistics/Neural_Network_Simple.qmd >}}


## Architecture {#sec-Neural_Network_Architecture}
A neural network is organized into layers (see @fig-Neural_Network_Simple): an input layer (the blue circles in the figure) that receives the data, one or more hidden layers (the orange circles in the figure) that transform the data through learned representations, and an output layer (the green circles in the figure) that produces predictions. Each neuron in a layer receives inputs, applies a weighted sum, adds a bias term, and passes the result through an activation function. For example, a simple network for predicting whether a student will pass an exam might take input features (hours studied, previous test scores) in the input layer, process them through hidden layers, and output a probability of passing.

The activation function introduces non-linearity into the network, allowing it to learn complex patterns. Common activation functions include the sigmoid function (which outputs values between 0 and 1), the hyperbolic tangent (tanh), and the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), which outputs the input if positive and zero otherwise. Without these non-linear activations, even deep networks would be equivalent to simple linear models.

To determine the performance of a neural network, we typically use a loss function that quantifies the difference between the predicted outputs and the true outputs. Common loss functions include mean squared error (MSE) for regression tasks and cross-entropy loss for classification tasks.
